evidence_quotes.quote: The public actors in Oosterwold decided not to install a centralised sewage system. Without a sewage system, the public actors enabled citizens to develop the site incrementally.
Section 10.33 of the EMA imposes a municipal duty to collect and transport wastewater by a sewage system within the municipal territory.
The public actors obliged residents to sign an anterior agreement in which residents agree to collect, treat and dispose of wastewater, as a prerequisite for residing in Oosterwold.

Furthermore, 19 key actor interviews served to develop a detailed description of Oosterwold and wastewater management, to cross-check the findings and to identify the experience of the residents and public actors (Weiss 1995).
At the beginning of the project, one measurement showed that 28 of 40 OSSFs failed to meet these requirements.
From now on, residents who operate an effective OSSF system may keep it; however, future residents and residents with inadequate OSSFs will be connected to the sewage system.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household wastewater/sanitation service delivery and sewer connection access in the Oosterwold urban development (Almere, the Netherlands), where public authorities withheld centralised municipal sewerage and required residents to self-provide onsite sewage facilities (OSSFs) before later mandating municipal sewer connections for non-compliant and future households.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain reading, it examines EU, national, provincial, and municipal environmental and water governance and legal frameworks. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, it directly analyses concrete rule-type mechanisms governing household sanitation access and service responsibility: the statutory municipal sewer-provision mandate and provincial waiver rule (Section 10.33 of the Dutch Environmental Management Act), experimental regulatory derogations under the Crisis and Recovery Act, mandatory anterior residency agreements requiring plot buyers to self-provide wastewater treatment as a condition of residence, water board discharge permitting rules (requiring Category III OSSFs), compliance inspections/enforcement, pollution vs. sewer cost-recovery levies, and administrative accommodation/reversal restoring municipal sewer connections.
criterion_notes.c3: Empirical socio-legal case study triangulating doctrinal legal analysis, systematic document analysis of municipal plans, permits, land transfer, anterior, and water agreements, 3 pilot interviews and 19 semi-structured key-actor interviews (residents, lawyers, policymakers, project members, environmental specialists), and administrative water-board OSSF inspection data (n=40 and n=199 OSSFs). Qualitative/case-study empirical socio-legal studies are eligible for systematic review inclusion.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports concrete outcomes relevant to sanitation service availability, connection, and reliability: initial exclusion from centralised municipal sewer infrastructure, near-universal household installation of individual OSSF III systems (rather than collective networks), high operational/regulatory failure rates of household systems (28 of 40 failing initially; 33 of 199 failing in November 2019) causing water/soil pollution, and the spring 2020 regulatory decision to connect residents with inadequate OSSFs and all future residents to the municipal sewage system.
criterion_notes.c5: Population/unit of analysis (resident households/plots in Oosterwold, Almere, with 199 inspected household OSSFs and 19 key-actor interviews), exposure (experimental legal/regulatory shift from mandatory municipal sewerage to resident-arranged OSSF provision under anterior agreements, discharge permits, and omitted provincial waiver), outcome (service delivery mode, OSSF failure/non-compliance rates, and eventual municipal sewer connection), and study design (empirical socio-legal case study) are all clearly identifiable.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is in English, an eligible language without translation.

study_design: Qualitative/mixed-methods socio-legal empirical case study (combining doctrinal legal analysis, policy/contract document analysis, 3 pilot and 19 semi-structured key-actor interviews, and administrative water-board OSSF compliance monitoring records)
population_and_sample: Resident households/plots and public institutional actors in the Oosterwold urban development area, Almere, the Netherlands (3 pilot interviews, 19 semi-structured key-actor interviews, policy/contract documents, and water board monitoring of 40 initial and 199 November 2019 household onsite sewage facilities).
exposure: Experimental legal and regulatory regime governing wastewater service provision in Oosterwold (derogation under the Crisis and Recovery Act, municipal decision not to install centralised sewerage without obtaining a provincial waiver under Section 10.33 of the Environmental Management Act, mandatory anterior residency agreements shifting wastewater provision to residents, water board discharge permits requiring OSSF III units, periodic enforcement inspections, and pollution levies).
outcome: Household wastewater service arrangement and sewer connection status (exclusion from centralised sewerage and near-universal adoption of individual OSSF III units rather than collective systems; household OSSF non-compliance/failure rates of 28/40 initially and 33/199 in November 2019 with deteriorating water quality; and the spring 2020 decision to connect non-compliant OSSF households and future residents to the municipal sewage system).
rationale: This socio-legal empirical case study satisfies all systematic review inclusion criteria under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. It examines household wastewater/sanitation service provision and municipal sewer connection in Oosterwold (Almere, the Netherlands), analysing concrete legal and regulatory rules governing service access and responsibility (the statutory municipal sewer duty and provincial waiver rules under EMA s. 10.33, Crisis and Recovery Act experimental rules, mandatory anterior residency agreements, water board discharge permits, inspections, and levies) using interviews, document analysis, and water board inspection data (28/40 and 33/199 OSSF failures), culminating in mandatory municipal sewer connections for non-compliant and future households.
